newsitem.title: UK: Britain says no return of Elgin marbles to Greece.
newsitem.headline: Britain says no return of Elgin marbles to Greece.

text.p: Britain's new Heritage Secretary Chris Smith on Sunday ruled out returning the Elgin marbles to Greece.
"We decided it was not a feasible or sensible option. We won't do it," Smith said on BBC television.

The return of the classical sculptures, brought to London nearly 200 years ago from Athens, has been a long-standing Greek demand, first put to the British government by the late actress and culture minister Melina Mercouri.
Hopes had risen in Greece that with Thursday's election of a new Labour government in Britain, the return of the treasures might now be closer at hand.
But Smith, whose ministry is responsible for cultural affairs, said the marbles were an integral part of the British Museum collection, visited by millions of people each year.
"It would make no sense at all to split up the British Museum collection in that way," he said. An entire room in the museum is dedicated to the marbles.

At the beginning of the 19th century, when greece was under Ottoman rule, Scottish peer Thomas Bruce made off with almost all the bas-reliefs from the Parthenon's frieze, most of its pedimental structures, and a caryatid from the Erectheion.
He sold these to London's British Museum in 1816.
Smith said returning the sculptures could encourage other countries to demand the return of their treasures, thereby unleashing a worldwide swapping system of precious art works.
Those who oppose their return to Greece say the British Museum safeguarded them from damage while other sculptures at the Acropolis temples suffered Athens' notorious air pollution.
